title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 211: The Wood Wide Web: Rethinking the Subterranean Forest
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 211 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

The Wood Wide Web: Rethinking the Subterranean Forest

Paragraph 1. For more than a hundred years, people thought trees in a forest fought each other alone for water, sunlight, and rich soil. Scientists believed that when one tree drank water, the tree beside it stayed dry. However, new studies in the past thirty years have changed this old idea completely. Today, scientists know that a huge underground network of tiny mushrooms, called fungi, connects different trees across the forest.

Paragraph 2. Trees and underground fungi help each other live. Trees use sunlight to make sweet food, and they send up to forty percent of their sugars down to the fungi. In return, the fungi grow millions of hair-thin threads through tiny spaces in the dirt. Thick tree roots cannot easily pick up minerals and water from hard ground alone, so the fungi bring these supplies back to the trees.

Paragraph 3. Canadian scientist Dr. Suzanne Simard proved that trees even share food through this underground web. Her team put plastic bags around branches of tall birch trees and small fir trees and added special carbon. The team saw carbon move both ways between the two tree species. In sunny summer days, birch trees sent extra food to young fir trees sitting in the dark shade. Later in autumn, when birch trees lost their leaves, green fir trees sent food back.

Paragraph 4. The underground web also works like a forest alarm system. When hungry insects attack one plant, healthy plants connected to the same fungal threads quickly make bad-tasting chemicals to protect themselves. Saving huge old 'mother trees' keeps this underground network alive so baby trees grow strong.
